Pankaj: ok so the plan. do contest problems every day. 3 a day minimum
Mahima: I was thinking of doing the app design project this month?
Pankaj: design is not a real path. contests are what companies notice
Mahima: I like the design side though

Pankaj: no. half effort = no result. do the problems first
Mahima: ok

(4 days later)

qa.q: What could Pankaj do to win Mahima back, and why?

subtype: Approach: pushing own path as the only path [Pitfall]
passage:
In the small engineering college outside Madurai, Rehana was famous for one thing: she had reached the national round of a competitive coding contest. So when the department paired her with Keerthana, a first-year, she knew exactly what to do.
'Two hundred problems by December,' she said, handing over a printed list. 'Arrays, then graphs, then dynamic programming. That's how I did it.'
Keerthana nodded. What she didn't say was that she spent her evenings redesigning the canteen's menu board on her phone, and loved it.
At their weekly meetings Keerthana showed Rehana a poster she had made for the cultural fest. Rehana glanced at it. 'Nice. But how many problems this week?'
'Twelve.'
'You need thirty.'
By October, Keerthana was making excuses to miss the meetings. By November she had stopped coming. Rehana told a friend the junior 'just wasn't serious'.

qa.q: What was on Rehana's printed list?
qa.a: Two hundred problems by December: arrays, then graphs, then dynamic programming.

qa.q: What does Rehana's comment that Keerthana 'just wasn't serious' suggest about Rehana?
qa.a: It suggests Rehana feels frustrated and sure her own path is the only real one, missing that Keerthana's interest lay elsewhere.

qa.q: What could Rehana have asked at the first meeting?
qa.a: What Keerthana enjoys and hopes to do, then shape the plan around design, with coding only as far as needed.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the mentoring by November?
qa.a: Keerthana sees it as something that doesn't fit her at all, so she loses interest and stops coming.

grounding: Shows a mentor insisting her competitive coding route is the only way, though the junior loves design, until the junior loses interest and stops coming.

subtype: Approach: pushing own path as the only path [Pitfall]
passage:
At the university in São Paulo, Beatriz had won two programming contests and was proud of it. When she was assigned to mentor Camila, a first-year, she brought a plan: daily contest problems, weekend practice contests, a target ranking by June.
'But I'm more into interface design,' Camila said at their first coffee. 'I like making apps look and feel right.'
'Design is easy to pick up later,' Beatriz said. 'Algorithms are what companies test. Trust me, it worked for me.'
For a month Camila tried. She solved problems half-heartedly and kept sketching screens in the margins of her notebook. At each meeting Beatriz asked for her contest score and skipped past the sketches.
By April, Camila was cancelling meetings. In May she found a design student group and joined it. When Beatriz messaged, 'You've been quiet!', Camila replied with one line: 'I think I need a different kind of mentor.'

qa.q: What does Beatriz's 'Trust me, it worked for me' suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels confident, even proud, sure that her own path must suit anyone.

qa.q: What else could Beatriz have done after Camila mentioned design?
qa.a: Ask more about it and build a plan around design, with just enough algorithms for company tests.

qa.q: How does the mentoring feel to Camila by April?
qa.a: Camila feels unheard and uninterested, cancelling meetings because her sketches are always skipped.

grounding: Shows a mentor pushing her own competitive programming route on a junior who loves design, until the junior loses interest and seeks another mentor.
